title: Yesterday
job: Past tense — the first big divergence
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review of the romanization, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The past tense does not care who you are talking about — it cares about GENDER and NUMBER. The endings are -l for a man, -la for a woman, -lo for a thing that is neuter, and -li for more than one. So the same speaker writes Ya kupíl or Ya kupíla depending on who they are, and the verb says nothing about "I" at all. English marks none of this and gives you no habit to fall back on.
Because the past names a gender and not a person, vy always takes -li — Vy kupíli bilét? — even when it means one man. It is the same rule as M2's Vy ustáli?: vy takes the plural, always.

"To be" comes back. The present had no word at all, and the past has byl (m) · bylá (f) · býlo (n) · býli (pl) — and the stress moves as the ending does, which is why three of the four carry an acute and byl, having only the one syllable, carries none. This is the whole shape of Russian's "be": a real word in the past, a real word in the future (M6), and nothing in the present. "Russian has no verb to be" was never true — only its present tense is empty.

Russian verbs come in pairs, and yesterday's single finished events take the other half of the pair from the one M4 used: pit' becomes výpil, chitát' becomes prochitál, and pokupát' — which this course never writes — is the everyday partner of kupíl. They are separate words with separate dictionary entries, not endings on one verb. What decides which you use is whether you are reporting one completed event (these) or a habit or an unfinished stretch of time (a second past this level does not teach).
There is no did. Negation is still M3's one word in one place, now in front of the past verb: Vcherá ya ne kupíl khleb. Nothing is added, nothing moves, and the verb keeps the ending it had.

dóma means "at home" and domóy means "to home" — both are single words that take no preposition and no ending, which is why this level uses them: they say where and where-to without opening anything new.

sentences.cue: Yesterday I was at home (said by a man)

words.note: Yesterday. It usually opens the sentence, and every sentence on this rung is anchored by it. Never changes shape.

The past of "to be" — the verb that had no present-tense word at all. byl for a man, bylá for a woman, býlo for a neuter thing, býli for more than one and for vy. This one row is the whole story of Russian "be": nothing in the present, byl behind you, and búdu · búdete · búdet ahead of you — M6 builds the future out of them. Three tenses, one word, and only the middle one is empty.
"At home", in one word — no preposition, no ending, nothing to build. Its partner domóy means "homewards", and the pair covers being somewhere and going there without touching the case system at all.

sentences.trap: M1 said the present of "to be" is simply not written, and that was true — of the present. This sentence has a real word in it, and if you are a woman it is a different real word.
sentences.sound: fchee-RA ya byl DO-ma. byl is one tight syllable with the hard y vowel; the v of vcherá is said as an f.

variations.cue: Yesterday I was at home (said by a woman)
variations.changed: byl → bylá: the same sentence, said by a woman
vy takes býli, the plural shape, even for one person — and the question moves nothing

variations.cue: Yesterday I was not at home
variations.changed: ne in front of the verb — the same one word as in M3

mistake.why: yest' is not a past tense, and Russian's present "be" is written as nothing anyway. Yesterday needs byl — or bylá, depending on who is speaking.

sentences.usage: Saying where you were — and the first sentence in the course whose shape depends on your own gender.
sentences.mnemonic: The present is empty; the past is not. byl is a real word that had no present-tense twin.

sentences.cue: Yesterday I bought bread (said by a man)

words.note: "Bought", from kupít' — the half of the pair Russian uses for one finished purchase. The ending follows the buyer's gender: kupíl (m), kupíla (f), kupíli (more than one, and vy). The other half of the pair, pokupát', is for buying as a habit and this level does not write it. The shape kuplyú belongs here too: it looks like a present tense and it means "I will buy" (M6).

sentences.trap: khleb is unchanged, exactly as it was in M3 — a masculine thing keeps its shape as the object, in the past as in the present. The tense never touches the noun.
sentences.sound: fchee-RA ya koo-PEEL khlyep. The stress on kupíl is on the ending, and it stays there in kupíla too.

variations.cue: Yesterday I bought bread (said by a woman)
variations.changed: kupíl → kupíla: the ending follows who is speaking, not what was bought
swap the thing bought — the verb ending does not notice
vy takes kupíli, and the question adds nothing — there is no did

mistake.why: The "some of it" shape again, which this level does not teach. The plain object is khleb, past or present.

sentences.usage: Reporting what you did — the frame most of this rung is built on.
sentences.mnemonic: The ending looks at the person speaking, never at the thing bought.

sentences.cue: Yesterday I bought a newspaper (said by a woman)

words.note: Newspaper. Feminine, so it takes M3's -u ending as the object: gazétu. Two endings are moving in this sentence and they are answering to different things — kupíla to the speaker, gazétu to its job in the sentence.

sentences.trap: Two endings moving at once, for two different reasons. kupíla ends in -a because a woman is speaking; gazétu ends in -u because it is the thing bought. Neither has anything to do with the other, and reading one as agreeing with the other is the mistake this sentence exists to prevent.
sentences.sound: fchee-RA ya koo-PEE-la ga-ZYE-too. Four unstressed vowels flatten and two land hard — the ordinary Russian rhythm.

variations.cue: Yesterday I bought a newspaper (said by a man)
variations.changed: kupíla → kupíl: the speaker changed, and gazétu did not
swap the thing bought — the new noun is feminine too, so it bends the same way
a name instead of ya — and the ending still follows the woman, not the newspaper

mistake.why: gazéta is the subject shape. As the thing bought it is gazétu — M3's rule, still running underneath the new tense.

sentences.usage: The everyday errand sentence — and the clearest case of two endings answering to two different masters.
sentences.mnemonic: One ending looks at the speaker; the other looks at the job. They never consult each other.

sentences.cue: Yesterday I went home (said by a man)

words.note: "Went", in the sense of setting off — from poytí. Look at what happens to the yó: poshyól for a man, but poshlá for a woman, with that vowel gone altogether and the acute landing on whatever the new ending brought. The quiet Russian line keeps the two dots on that letter (ё); most Russian books leave them off and let you work it out. poydú is the same word again, and it means "I will go" (M6) even though it has no future-looking ending on it.
"To home". English uses one word — "home" — for both being there and going there; Russian splits them: dóma is where you are, domóy is where you are heading. Neither takes a preposition or an ending.

sentences.trap: dóma and domóy are one English word and two Russian ones, and swapping them says the opposite of what you mean. Vcherá ya poshyól dóma would be "yesterday I set off at home".
sentences.sound: fchee-RA ya pa-SHOL da-MOY. yó is always the stressed syllable of its word, wherever it appears, so its acute is part of the letter rather than a decision about the word — you never have to work out where poshyól is stressed.

variations.cue: Yesterday I went home (said by a woman)
variations.changed: poshyól → poshlá: the yó disappears completely when the ending changes, and the acute moves onto the vowel that replaced it
M4's time word hangs off the end without disturbing anything
vy takes poshlí — and again the question adds no word

mistake.why: dóma is where you are, not where you go. Setting off for home is domóy.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody how your evening ended — and the sentence that makes the yó policy worth having.
sentences.mnemonic: yó is always the stressed vowel of its word. Lose the yó and the acute simply lands on whatever vowel the new ending brought.

sentences.cue: Yesterday I drank coffee (said by a man)

words.note: "Drank" — one cup, finished. It is a different word from M4's pit', not a past tense of it: the vy- on the front is what makes it a single completed act. pit' is what you do every morning; výpit' is what you did once yesterday.

sentences.trap: M4's p'yu has no past tense of its own on this rung. Reporting yesterday's coffee means reaching for a different word, and that is the single hardest habit in Russian for an English speaker to build.
sentences.sound: fchee-RA ya VY-peel KO-fye. The stress jumps to the front on výpil — the vy- prefix pulls it there, which is unusual and worth noticing.

variations.cue: Yesterday I drank coffee (said by a woman)
variations.changed: výpil → výpila: the speaker's gender, once again
swap the drink — the object is masculine either way, so nothing bends

variations.cue: In the morning I drink coffee
variations.changed: the habit version, with M4's verb — a different word for a different kind of drinking

mistake.why: Not wrong Russian — a different meaning. pil is "was drinking" or "used to drink", the unfinished kind; one finished cup yesterday is výpil.

sentences.usage: Reporting one particular thing you drank — and the module's clearest look at the verb pairs.
sentences.mnemonic: pit' is the habit, výpit' is the cup. Two words, not two tenses.

sentences.cue: Yesterday I read a book (said by a man)

words.note: "Read", and finished it — from prochitát', M4's chitát' with pro- on the front. The prefix is what turns reading into having-read: with it the book is done, without it you were simply reading. Same gender endings as every other past verb.

sentences.trap: The English "I read a book yesterday" leaves it open whether you finished. Russian does not: prochitál says you got to the end, and chitál would say you were at it.
sentences.sound: fchee-RA ya pra-chee-TAL KNEE-goo. Three unstressed syllables before the stress lands — say them light and quick.

variations.cue: Yesterday I read a book (said by a woman)
variations.changed: prochitál → prochitála, following the reader
swap what was read — and it bends, being feminine
vy takes prochitáli, and the question is made by the mark alone

mistake.why: Correct Russian for a different fact: that says you were reading, not that you finished. For a book you got through, prochitál.

sentences.usage: Reporting something you completed — and the same pro- trick works on a good many verbs.
sentences.mnemonic: The prefix is the finishing line. pro- means you crossed it.

sentences.cue: Yesterday I didn't buy sugar (said by a man)

words.note: Sugar. Masculine, ends in a consonant, and never changes as the object — the same free ride as khleb and sok.

sentences.trap: English builds a whole new verb shape for this — "did not buy", with the past moving onto "did" and "buy" going back to its plain form. Russian changes nothing at all: ne goes in front of kupíl and the sentence is finished.
sentences.sound: fchee-RA ya nye koo-PEEL SA-khar. The final r of sákhar is a light tap, not the English r.

variations.cue: Yesterday I didn't buy sugar (said by a woman)
variations.changed: ne does not protect the verb from its ending — kupíla still follows the speaker
drop ne and nothing else has to move back
vy takes kupíli, and ne sits in the same place it always sits

mistake.why: The English shape, where the past moves onto a helper and the main verb goes back to its dictionary form. Russian keeps the past on the verb: ne kupíl.

sentences.usage: Saying what you failed to do — and the cleanest proof that Russian has no did.
sentences.mnemonic: No helper, no reset. ne kupíl is the whole of "did not buy".

sentences.cue: Yesterday I bought a ticket (said by a man)

words.note: Ticket — for a train, a plane, a museum, a concert. Masculine, so it does not change as the object. Its other two shapes belong to counting: dva biléta, and biléty for more than one (M8).

sentences.trap: There is still no word for "a". Vcherá ya kupíl bilét is "a ticket" and "the ticket" alike, and M10 will show how word order settles it when it matters.
sentences.sound: fchee-RA ya koo-PEEL bee-LYET. The e after l softens it, so the ending is "lyet", not "let".

variations.cue: Yesterday I bought a ticket (said by a woman)
variations.changed: the speaker's ending again — the ticket has nothing to do with it
vy takes kupíli, and the question adds no word at all

variations.cue: I want to buy a ticket
variations.changed: back to M3's frame — after khochú the verb stands in its dictionary shape, kupít'

mistake.why: Not wrong, but it says "one ticket" as a count rather than "a ticket". Russian has no article, so the bare noun is the ordinary sentence.

sentences.usage: Travel, museums, concerts — and the third variation is the sentence you will actually need at the counter.
sentences.mnemonic: Still no articles. The bare noun does both jobs.

words.note: Rain — and here it is the SUBJECT of the sentence, which is why byl takes the masculine ending. dozhd' ends in the soft sign — the ' this romanization writes for it — and M1 warned that a soft-sign noun can be either gender: this one is masculine, and there is no way to tell from the spelling. Learn each soft-sign noun with its gender.

sentences.trap: There is no "it" anywhere. English needs a subject that means nothing — "it rained" — and Russian makes the rain itself the subject, so byl agrees with dozhd'. The verb follows whatever noun the sentence is about: if it had been about sneg (snow), also masculine, byl would still be right, and a feminine subject would take bylá.
sentences.sound: fchee-RA byl dozhd'. The final -zhd' is a single squeezed sound ending soft; it is the hardest word on this rung to say.

variations.cue: Yesterday it rained in the evening
variations.changed: M4's time word at the end — nothing else moves
saying it did not happen takes a different shape of both words — ne býlo, and dozhdyá. This level does not teach that shape; it is here so you recognise it
swap the time — and byl still agrees with dozhd', not with anybody speaking

mistake.why: The English "it" smuggled in. Russian has no dummy subject: the rain is the subject, and byl agrees with it.

sentences.usage: Weather — the most-used small talk in the language, and the sentence where the gender rule stops being about people.
sentences.mnemonic: The verb agrees with whatever the sentence is about. Sometimes that is the rain.

words.note: Letter — the kind you write, and also a letter of an alphabet in the plural. Neuter, ending in -o, so it does not change as the object: neuter nouns never do.

sentences.trap: prochitáli is plural because vy is always plural — not because more than one person read it. The past tense never names a person, only a gender and a number, and vy hands it the number.
sentences.sound: vy pra-chee-TA-lee pees'-MO. The ' inside pis'mó softens the s; the stress is on the last syllable, which is where most neuter -o nouns keep it.

variations.changed: swap the thing read — and this one bends, being feminine
the answer, from a man — prochitál, the singular masculine ending
ne in front of the verb — a perfectly ordinary question, not a reproach

mistake.why: vy takes the plural ending in the past, always: prochitáli, however few people you mean.

sentences.usage: Checking whether somebody has done something — and the last of the module's four gender endings.
sentences.mnemonic: vy is plural in every tense. The past is no exception.

comprehensionPool.cue: Yesterday I was at home (a woman speaking)
Yesterday it rained in the morning
